Abstract
In the rapidly evolving field of agriculture, the integration of autonomous systems is essential for enhancing productiv-
ity and efficiency. This study addresses the challenge of navigation line extraction in autonomous agricultural robots, a 
critical component for precise field operations. In this study, three deep learning-based semantic segmentation models, 
ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet, were trained on corn crop row images to extract the traversable path of the robot. Then, 
we proposed a novel navigation line extraction algorithm based on the Douglas–Peucker algorithm which uses the 
output mask from the semantic segmentation to extract the centre navigation line for robot guidance. The results of 
the experiments showed that PSPNet achieved the highest mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 96.50%, followed by 
Deeplabv3+ (96.30%) and ENet (95.13%). While ENet showed more consistent performance across various lighting condi-
tions, the novel algorithm demonstrated remarkable accuracy, reducing angle errors to an average of 1.1°, 1.6°, and 1.6° 
for ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet, respectively, compared to 4.6°, 4.9°, and 6.7° using the baseline method. This improve-
ment is critical for ensuring precise and stable robot navigation in agricultural fields. Beyond its technical contributions, 
this study offers practical implications for real-world deployment, ensuring reliable operation in dynamic agricultural 
environments. By addressing limitations in conventional navigation techniques, the proposed method enhances robot 
maneuverability in corn crop fields, particularly under challenging lighting conditions. However, its application across 
different crop types and terrains, further optimizing real-time processing efficiency, are yet to be explored. This work 
represents a significant step toward achieving robust, autonomous navigation in precision agriculture.

1  Introduction

Key indicators of modern agricultural progress include the optimal use of agricultural resources, maximized production, 
and overall development [4]. In the United States, a crucial aspect of modern agricultural production is the autonomy 
and intelligence of machinery and equipment. Advancing highly intelligent agricultural machinery is a key focus of cur-
rent agricultural development efforts. The mechanization, automation, and informatization of agricultural equipment

ogy is autonomous navigation, which allows robotic platforms to function in the field without human intervention. 
Autonomous navigation as a critical capability for agricultural robots, allows them to navigate and operate along crop 
rows autonomously [6, 7]. To enable this functionality, the robot must be able to extract the navigation line within field 
environments and follow it precisely [8]. This study addresses the common field navigation challenge of extracting the 
navigation line by detecting crop rows in a cornfield.
Navigating row crop fields presents uncertainties such as weed density, variable light conditions, growth stages, and 
crop row discontinuities. Many proposed solutions involve using the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) along with 
costly sensors mounted on the robot, such as three-dimensional multi-channel Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) [9, 
10]. However, GNSS alone lacks sufficient accuracy, potentially causing robots to damage crops. The accuracy and stability 
of RTK-GNSS can be compromised by factors like satellite signal loss, fix-solution failure, and differential stream discon-
nection. Furthermore, expensive sensors not only increase the robot’s cost but are also prone to failure under harsh field 
conditions, such as high temperatures, humidity, and dust. While LiDAR is vital for autonomous driving in urban areas 
where obstacles are typically hard and well-defined, its application in agriculture is limited due to the natural differences 
in the environment. The complex and soft nature of obstacles like leaves and stems, which are close to the UGV, make it 
challenging to use LiDAR effectively. These sensors only measure distance and lack the ability to detect colour informa-
tion, falling short in meeting the demands of complex farmland environments [5, 11]. Visual navigation technology, on 
the other hand, uses cameras to capture images of the farmland and processes these images to obtain navigation paths. 
This technology offers extensive detection capabilities, comprehensive information acquisition and cost benefits [12].
Detecting crop rows is essential for developing vision-based navigation for agricultural robots. Enhancing computer 
vision algorithms to extract crop row baselines swiftly and accurately is a key area for advancement [5, 13]. Computer 
vision sensors are often more cost-effective [14] than Real-Time Kinematic Global Positioning Systems (RTK‐GPS) and 
other costly navigation hardware used in agricultural robots, providing a dependable method to gain navigation infor-
mation through cameras. However, traditional computer vision algorithms struggle to address a range of issues in real 
farmland settings, such as varying light conditions, shadow occlusion, and clutter interference, leading to inaccuracies 
in road segmentation and navigation. In recent years, deep learning has seen rapid advancements in computer vision, 
particularly with the convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithms and has produced significant results [5, 15]. CNN 
algorithms have successfully addressed major challenges in implementing vision-based navigation systems. They are 
widely used in various agricultural vision tasks, yielding promising outcomes [16, 17]. Neural networks possess strong 
learning capabilities, enabling them to account for various real-world farmland scenarios within the pre-training data-
set and effectively handle issues caused by light, shadows, or debris with high robustness. In deep learning navigation, 
field crops or branches were first detected using deep learning object detection networks, and navigation paths were 
extracted from the line of objects. Extracting corn stalks to fit the navigation line significantly improved navigation accu-
racy compared to traditional machine learning techniques [18]. In vineyards, De Aguiar et al. [19] used deep learning 
algorithms like MobileNet, Inception, and YOLO to detect grape trunks for field autonomous navigation. Yang et al. [20] 
applied the faster region-based convolutional neural network (faster-RCNN) to identify maize rhizomes and then used 
the least square method to fit the navigation line based on the identified maize rhizome positions, achieving accurate 
planning of the maize crop field path.
Compared to object detection, the semantic segmentation method is more suitable for extracting navigation lines. 
Agricultural environments present challenges such as diverse forms, complex backgrounds, and varying light condi-
tions, which traditional graphic methods struggle to address. Deep learning-based semantic segmentation is a powerful 
image processing technique that performs well in complex agricultural settings. Zhou et al. [21] utilized an expanded 
convolutional neural network with a global context to identify and extract roads from UAV aerial images. Lan et al. [22] 
introduced a neural network architecture consisting of two encoders and a decoder network to segment and extract 
roads. Kim et al. [23] applied a patch-based CNN for path area segmentation in orchards, which involves cropping image 
patches, generating a path score map, and classifying paths; they then used boundary line determination for path detec-
tion. Lin and Chen [24] trained a neural network for semantic segmentation in a tea garden and subsequently employed 
the Hough transform to delineate lines between tea garden shrubs. These innovative methods are practical in specific 
scenarios. However, there has been limited research on high-precision segmentation in unstructured environments and 
the extraction of navigation lines. To this end, we propose a novel navigation line extraction algorithm which accurately 
predicts the crop row centre line in any field condition including various crop growth stages, lighting condition, presence 
of weed and other obstacles without requiring any condition-specific tuning, using the predicted crop row segmenta-
tion mask from the semantic segmentation model. Also, opposed to the manual method of annotating ground truth

2  Related works
A visual navigation system is a crucial component of agricultural robots. An effective visual navigation system enables 
these robots to understand their environment using advanced intelligent or artificial intelligence algorithms to process 
and analyse collected images. This capability allows robots to perceive and interpret their surroundings, achieving 
intelligence and autonomy in mechanical operations. The vision system of a robot initially captures a two-dimensional 
image of the three-dimensional external environment using an image acquisition device, such as a camera. The two-
dimensional image is then processed by intelligent algorithms to perform image segmentation, feature extraction, and 
other image understanding tasks [25]. Ultimately, this process yields a symbolic representation of the image, aiding 
agricultural robots in making decisions for subsequent actions. A flowchart illustrating the above processes can be seen 
in Fig. 1. Studies which investigated different approaches to visual navigation of agricultural robots are discussed in the 
following subsections.
2.1  Traditional/classical computer vision techniques
For visual navigation, agricultural robots need to segment digital images into distinct regions with unique properties 
using image segmentation algorithms to identify the locations and boundary points of objects within the images [26, 
27]. A traditional segmentation technique such as the colour-index-based segmentation method, converts RGB space 
into an alternative colour space to generate high-contrast gray images, thereby highlighting the plant pixel regions

(ExR), and Excess Green minus Excess Red Index (ExGR), typically rely on the green channel information, which can fail

image segmentation approach is machine learning-based segmentation, which employs machine learning algorithms to 
learn common attributes of objects in the image and then classify pixels with the same characteristics into the same class

[33], Random Forest (RF) [34], support vector machine (SVM) [35], and decision tree-based segmentation model (DTSM) 
[36]. However, due to the environmental complexity and crop diversity in actual agricultural scenarios, it is challenging 
to achieve the desired segmentation results using only underlying feature information. Deep learning techniques can 
capture global feature information in images and establish a one-to-one mapping between semantic categories and 
image pixels, leading to improved segmentation results [37, 38].
2.2  Semantic segmentation techniques
Semantic segmentation, a crucial aspect of deep learning, is extensively applied in agriculture [39, 40] for effectively 
segmenting and extracting paths between crop rows. It involves assigning each pixel in an image to a specific object 
class. In autonomous driving, semantic segmentation is used to identify environmental objects like roads, pedestrians, 
vehicles, and traffic signs, creating a detailed scene map. This data is then used to plan the vehicle’s trajectory, ensuring 
safe and efficient driving. Recent advancements in algorithms have significantly improved the accuracy and speed of 
pixel-level semantic segmentation [41]. Fully convolutional networks (FCN) [42] first introduced convolutional neural 
networks to semantic segmentation in 2015, utilizing convolutional layers instead of fully connected layers to accommo-
date any input size. Multi-scale information fusion further enhanced network performance, achieving an mIoU of 62.2% 
on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset. PSPNet [43] introduced a novel spatial pyramid pooling module (SPP) that combines 
feature maps to capture contextual information at different scales, resulting in an mIoU of 85.4% on the PASCAL VOC 2012 
dataset. DeepLabv3 [44] integrates the advantages of the encoder-decoder structure with the spatial pyramid pooling 
module, effectively encoding contextual information and more accurately restoring boundaries, achieving an mIoU of 
85.7% on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
Various studies have applied different neural network architectures for the semantic segmentation of agricultural fields 
to identify pathways for robots. Zhang et al. [45] proposed a Fast-Unet model for navigation path recognition between 
rows of fruit trees to improve recognition accuracy and inference speed. Their study achieved a Mean Intersection over 
Union (mIoU) of 0.977, 0.987, and 0.956 for peaches, oranges, and kiwifruits navigation path extraction, respectively. Li 
et al. [46] proposed VC-UNet, a lightweight semantic segmentation model to detect oilseed rape row for infield naviga-
tion of agri-robot. The proposed model enhances the UNet model, with VGG16 replacing the original backbone feature 
extraction network of UNet and convolutional block attention module (CBAM) integrated at the upsampling stage to 
enhance focus on segmentation targets. This study demonstrated an average accuracy of 94.11%. Bakken et al. [47] 
developed a CNN-based semantic segmentation network for crop row detection, which trains the network with noisy 
labels, allowing the robot to adapt to seasonal and crop changes effectively. This network’s segmentation accuracy facili-
tates the vision-based movement of agricultural robots along crop rows. Song et al. [6] proposed an automatic wheat 
segmentation method based on FCN and navigation line extraction, achieving a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 
95% to enhance the accuracy and robustness of navigation lines in wheat fields. Cao et al. [5] introduced a visual naviga-
tion method using an improved ENet semantic segmentation network model for row segmentation in farmland images. 
They utilized the trained semantic segmentation network to extract and classify feature points from the segmentation 
results. The experimental results indicated that the algorithm is highly adaptable to farmland images in diverse condi-
tions, achieving a crop row detection accuracy of 90.9%. De Silva et al. [14] utilized the UNet semantic segmentation 
network model for crop row detection, training the model on both RGB-only and RGB-D datasets. Their results showed 
that the peak validation intersection over union (IoU) was 22.5% for the RGB-only model and 31.75% for the RGB-D model. 
Additionally, they reported an individual IoU variation between 10 and 50% in their test dataset. Despite the lower IoU 
scores, their postprocessing algorithm was able to accurately recover crop rows for navigation and detect crop rows in 
challenging field conditions. Yu et al. [10] evaluated various semantic segmentation-based computer vision methods,

2.3  Navigation line extraction techniques
Besides computational methods based on filtering and segmentation, line detection and fitting methods can also be 
employed to extract farm or orchard road navigation lines in machine vision-based automatic navigation systems for 
agricultural robots and vehicles. Currently, the most commonly used line fitting and detection algorithms include Hough 
transform, least squares method, particle swarm clustering algorithm [48], and Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) 
[49]. The Hough transform is the most frequently used line detection algorithm in image analysis and machine vision 
processing [50]. It offers strong robustness and noise resistance, but its significant computational demands can affect the 
real-time performance of autonomous navigation. Jiang et al. [51] utilized the Hough transform to detect wheat rows in 
early growth stages under complex natural conditions. Li et al. [1] implemented an improved Hough transform method 
based on a subdivision algorithm to effectively extract robot paths. Recently, Zhao et al. [52] introduced the Deep Hough 
Transform method, an end-to-end framework that combines convolutional layers for feature extraction with the Hough 
transform for detecting semantic lines. Panda et al. [53] applied the deep Hough transform to detect semantic lines in 
agricultural field images. Their experimental results demonstrated relatively good performance of the semantic line 
detection model on both ground and aerial images. Despite the promising outcomes, the Hough transform and deep 
Hough transform are only suitable for scenes with prominent line marks. In agricultural fields, however, road edges are 
irregular and lack clear straight-line marks, rendering this technique unsuitable.
The least squares method is another widely used approach for line detection in agricultural environments. The princi-
ple of least squares involves finding the best functional match for the data by minimizing the sum of squares of the fitting 
errors [54]. Compared to the Hough transform, the least squares algorithm features a simpler and more straightforward 
formula, faster detection speed, and higher accuracy [55]. Consequently, the least squares-based linear fitting algorithm 
is extensively employed in the real-time extraction of visual navigation lines. The RANSAC algorithm is a robust model 
estimation method frequently used in curve fitting and image processing. By applying the RANSAC algorithm, edge 
information points are eliminated to obtain the optimal interior-point set, allowing the visual navigation line to be fit-
ted using any line fitting technique. Some studies combine both the RANSAC and least squares methods to derive the 
navigation line. Cao et al. [5] proposed an improved random sampling consensus algorithm to extract the navigation 
line and then used the least-squares method to fit the navigation line. Their proposed algorithm was able to extract the 
navigation line with an accuracy of 91.2%. Li et al. [46] used the least squares method to fit the centerline of oilseed rape 
crop rows achieving an average yaw angle deviation of 3.76°, with a pixel average offset of 6.13 pixels. Similarly, Zhang 
et al. [45] utilised the least squares method to fit navigation lines between rows of fruit trees. They reported mean dif-
ferences between the predicted yaw angle of peaches, oranges, and kiwifruits navigation paths and the labelled to be 
0.397°, 0.102°, and 0.239°, respectively. Asides the above well-known techniques, other studies have adopted different 
techniques to successfully extract navigation lines. De Silva et al. [14] used the triangle scan method (TSM) to determine 
the line parameters of the central crop row which the robot has to follow. The authors reported an average angular error of 
2.15° of their proposed technique. Liu et al. [56] proposed a modified shortest distance algorithm to fit pineapple crop row 
centerline and calculate the optimal navigation line. The proposed method achieved an angle error of 3.54°. Song et al. 
[6] used the RANSAC algorithm to fit the navigation line. Their method achieved an angle deviation of approximately 2°.
Despite the supposed robustness of the RANSAC algorithm, it can be inconsistent as the results can vary depending 
on the random samples chosen, leading to potential inconsistencies in line extraction. In addition, it requires careful 
selection of thresholds and other parameters to balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Considering 
the above-mentioned drawbacks of the line extraction algorithms, Yu et al. [10] adopted a polygon fitting method based 
on the Douglas–Peucker algorithm, to extract the navigation line given its efficiency and robustness. The proposed tech-
nique fits a polygon to the segmented path which could be a triangle or trapezoid and then calculates the midpoints of

3  Materials and methods
The method proposed in this study for extracting navigation paths between crop rows involves three main steps: (i) data 
annotation to generate training labels, (ii) semantic segmentation using ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet neural network 
models to perform pixel-level recognition of information between rows in corn crop images and obtain the correspond-
ing mask regions, and (iii) navigation line extraction based on the output mask from the semantic segmentation process, 
employing a novel line extraction algorithm. The flowchart of the proposed navigation pipeline is shown in Fig. 2.
3.1  Dataset
This study utilizes RGB image data obtained from a dataset in a publicly available repository containing crop row images 
collected by Sivakumar et al. [57] from corn fields across Illinois and Indiana using the TerraSentia robot (EarthSense Inc.), 
at a resolution of 1280 × 720 pixels. According to Sivakumar et al. [57], the RGB dataset was captured using a front-facing 
RGB camera mounted on the robot. It includes images from various growth stages (early, middle, and full growth) and 
under different lighting conditions (normal, bright, and dark light), as well as variations in appearance and occlusion. 
Additionally, the dataset features images taken while the robot navigated in a zig-zag pattern to provide a wider range 
of scenarios that could be encountered during autonomous driving. These variations enhance the robustness of deep 
learning models, leading to improved accuracy in diverse environments. The repository contains a total of 25,296 corn 
images. However, only 1030 images were carefully selected for this study while taking into account the different variations 
in the dataset as described earlier. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and testing sets in the proportions 
of 70%, 20%, and 10%, respectively, ensuring that each split contained unique data. In the training dataset, the propor-
tions of the corn crop growth stages were 48% for full growth, 20% for middle growth, and 32% for early growth. Figure 3 
illustrates the different variations of the dataset used for training the models.

3.2  Data annotation
To enhance scene understanding during autonomous navigation in the field, a dense annotation strategy was adopted 
to annotate the dataset. The annotated classes were chosen based on the needs for robot navigation within the crop 
rows. Consequently, 1030 images were manually annotated into two classes: (i) ground, representing the traversable path 
for the robot, and (ii) background, representing the non-traversable path, including crops, sky, and other scene features. 
A single annotator handled all annotations to ensure precise class boundaries and consistency. The Computer Vision 
Annotation Tool (CVAT, CVAT.ai Corporation) from Intel was used for all annotations, which considered both single-row 
and multiple-row images as seen in Fig. 4.

tion techniques used in this study included both colour and geometric transformations. Colour transformations involved

3.4  Semantic segmentation and model selection
In visual navigation, the accuracy of scene segmentation is crucial as it directly influences the subsequent extraction of 
navigation lines, ultimately determining the accuracy of computer vision navigation. Semantic segmentation, particularly 
for tasks like crop row segmentation for autonomous navigation, involves classifying each pixel in an image to identify 
specific regions such as crop rows and pathways. Accurately delineating road areas is a primary research focus. This study 
employs neural networks for road segmentation, utilizing various models in semantic segmentation to achieve high 
accuracy in identifying navigable paths within agricultural fields. For the purpose of this study, three different semantic 
segmentation neural network models, ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet were selected based on their performance in 
semantic segmentation tasks as discussed in the earlier sections of this paper. The architectures and advantages of these 
models are explained in the following subsections.
3.4.1  ENet
ENet is a lightweight, real-time semantic segmentation network optimized for accuracy and computational efficiency [58]. 
Its architecture comprises an initialization stage and five bottleneck stages—three for encoding and two for decoding. 
Each bottleneck block contains three convolutional layers: a 1 × 1 projection layer, a main convolutional layer (regular, 
dilated, deconvolutional, or asymmetric), and a 1 × 1 expansion layer, with batch normalization and PReLU applied 
between them. Downsampling uses max pooling, while decoding employs max-unpooling and spatial convolution 
without bias. Inspired by ResNet, ENet incorporates residual connections, reducing parameters and computational load 
[58]. Techniques such as asymmetric and dilated convolutions enhance efficiency, while a final deconvolution mod-
ule dominates the decoder’s processing time. Unlike symmetric encoder-decoder networks, ENet prioritizes efficient 
feature extraction, maintaining high-resolution feature maps to improve speed and accuracy. The omission of batch

3.4.2  Deeplabv3+
DeepLabv3+ is a semantic segmentation model designed to combine the advantages of spatial pyramid pooling and 
encoder-decoder structures. The model employs Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) to capture multi-scale contextual 
information and integrates a simple yet effective decoder module for recovering object boundaries [44]. By applying 
atrous convolutions, DeepLabv3+ controls the density of encoder features, balancing computational resources with 
segmentation accuracy. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like PASCAL VOC 2012 and 
Cityscapes, demonstrating its effectiveness in precise segmentation tasks [44]. ResNet101, used as the backbone for 
DeepLabv3+ in this study instead of the commonly used Xception network, offers significant advantages. ResNets, known 
for their residual blocks with shortcut connections, address the vanishing gradient problem in deep networks, allowing 
for the training of very deep architectures [59]. While the Xception network leverages depthwise separable convolutions 
for efficiency, ResNet101 provides a robust balance of depth and computational efficiency, making it more suitable for 
capturing complex features and finer details required in semantic segmentation. Compared to other ResNet variants, 
ResNet101 offers an optimal depth, balancing performance and resource consumption, which makes it preferable for 
tasks needing high accuracy and detailed segmentation boundaries.
3.4.3  PSPNet
In the paper by Zhao et al. [43], the Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet) is introduced as a powerful framework for 
semantic segmentation tasks. PSPNet incorporates a pyramid pooling module that captures global context information, 
enhancing the network’s ability to understand complex scenes. This unique architecture allows PSPNet to effectively 
combine local and global features, leading to more accurate pixel-level predictions. Using ResNet101 as its backbone, 
PSPNet benefits from deep supervision, improving segmentation accuracy. The pyramid pooling module efficiently 
collects information across different image regions, outperforming traditional global pooling methods. Additionally, 
ResNet101’s skip connections enable better learning of residuals, enhancing fine detail capture. PSPNet’s architecture is 
particularly suited for crop row segmentation, as it excels in precise boundary delineation and contextual understanding, 
making it valuable for autonomous agricultural robots.
3.5  Model training strategy
The training and validation of all models were conducted using the Pete Supercomputer of the High-Performance Com-
puting Centre (HPCC) at Oklahoma State University (OSU). The models were trained on GPU nodes, each equipped with at 
least two NVIDIA Quadro RTX6000 GPUs, totalling 22 GPUs. The training process utilized pre-divided datasets, consisting 
of 721 training images and 206 validation images, and was implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework. 
The cross entropy (CE) loss function and the Adam optimiser were employed during training. Hyperparameters included 
a learning rate of 1e−4, weight decay of 1e−5, and a learning rate decay coefficient of 0.1. The neural networks were 
trained for 50 epochs with a batch size of 4. This study adopted three training methods: transfer learning, fine-tuning, 
and training from scratch. The performance of these methods for the three different models was compared and evalu-
ated to determine the best model and training method.
3.5.1  Transfer learning
Deep learning methods depend significantly on large datasets with high-quality labels for optimal performance [60–64]. 
Preparing sufficient labelled data is labour-intensive, inefficient, and costly. Models with many parameters may not train 
well with insufficient data, leading to poor performance and overfitting. Transfer learning offers a viable solution for 
training complex models with limited data. It transfers knowledge from a source domain to a target domain for specific 
tasks [65, 66], utilising pretrained weights to improve performance and accelerate model convergence, even with limited 
training data [67]. In this paper, the backbone network of the models utilized pretrained weights on the ImageNet dataset 
which is a comprehensive image database containing 14,197,122 annotated images used for computer vision tasks. The 
source domain in this research work was the ImageNet dataset while the target domain was the navigation path dataset

3.5.2  Fine tuning
Fine-tuning is a variant of transfer learning where the pre-trained model undergoes additional training on a new dataset 
or task. Unlike standard transfer learning, fine-tuning involves unfreezing some or all layers of the pre-trained model, 
allowing them to be modified during training on the new task. This process updates all model parameters, including 
those of the pre-trained layers, enabling the model to learn task-specific details while preserving its general knowledge. 
Fine-tuning is particularly effective for domain-specific tasks where adapting a pre-trained model can enhance perfor-
mance. However, it demands more computational resources and time compared to transfer learning. In this study, the 
fine-tuning technique was explored and implemented by unfreezing all the layers of the pretrained backbone network 
(encoder) allowing its learned weights to be trained and updated alongside the weights and parameters of the decoder, 
while retaining the general knowledge of the pretrained model.
3.5.3  Scratch training
Training a model from scratch involves randomly initializing all model parameters and then optimizing them using a 
chosen optimization algorithm, such as the Adam optimizer used in this study, on a specific dataset. This approach allows 
complete flexibility in designing the model architecture and initializing parameters, enabling customization tailored 
to the task at hand. Training from scratch eliminates any biases or assumptions present in pre-trained models, which 
can be advantageous for tasks requiring unbiased learning. This method provides full control over every aspect of the 
training process, allowing for fine-tuning of hyperparameters and optimization strategies for the specific dataset and 
task. However, it can be computationally expensive and time-consuming, particularly for complex architectures and 
large datasets. Additionally, it often requires a significant amount of labelled data for deeper neural networks, such as 
Deeplabv3+, to achieve competitive performance, which may not always be feasible or available. This study, in addition 
to transfer learning and fine tuning, also explored the scratch training strategy for the three models to compare their 
performances to other training strategies implemented in this paper. In doing this, no pretrained weights were needed. 
All models were trained with all layers left unfrozen and without any source domain knowledge.

3.7  Navigation line extraction
After the semantic segmentation process is completed, the resulting segmentation mask is then used to extract the 
navigation line. This study adopted the Douglas–Peucker algorithm implemented in [10] as the baseline algorithm to 
extract the navigation line. In the baseline method, the algorithm is used to find convex polygons which are according 
to the shape of the path (segmentation mask). Afterwards, the midpoints of the polygon vertices are calculated and then 
averaged to get the overall midpoint of the polygon. This extracted midpoint is then used to obtain the navigation line. 
However, the calculation of a single midpoint of the polygon does not accurately reflect the curvature and orientation 
of the path. This results in a navigation line that may not be aligned correctly with the actual path, leading to potential 
navigation errors. To overcome this shortcoming, this study proposed an improved algorithm which accurately extracts 
the navigation line. The comparison between the baseline algorithm and the improved algorithm is detailed in the 
flowchart in Fig. 6. The steps involved in the proposed algorithm are explained in the following section.
3.7.1  Improved Douglas–Peucker algorithm
In view of the drawbacks associated with the baseline algorithm, an improved algorithm was proposed to accurately 
extract the navigation line for robot navigation. The improved algorithm entails polygon fitting as in the baseline 
algorithm, horizontal line scanning, multiple feature points extraction which accurately represents the curvature and 
orientation of the path, and finally the least squares fitting to obtain the navigation line. Figure 7 shows the pseu-
docode for the baseline method and the improved method. As in the baseline method, the algorithm fits a convex 
polygon to the shape of the path. Then, instead of calculating the midpoints of the polygon vertices and averaging 
these midpoints to obtain a single midpoint, the algorithm scans horizontally through the polygon mask at a speci-
fied interval to extract multiple feature points. The feature points extracted are the median pixels of each line scan. 
These extracted feature points provide a more detailed representation of the path. The scanning interval selected 
in this study was 20 pixels. Selecting too large interval means that the navigation line might miss finer details of the 
path because fewer scan lines mean fewer points will be considered in the line extraction process. This will eventu-
ally lead to a reduced accuracy given that the fitted line may not accurately represent the actual path. On the other 
hand, too small interval might make the method too sensitive to small variations or noise in the path, leading to a 
jagged or unstable navigation line. In addition, the computational cost will be increased, and the process slows down 
as more points are considered. Therefore, the best interval was selected from experimenting.

To assess the accuracy, stability, and robustness of the proposed crop row navigation line extraction algorithm 
based on three different neural networks, we conducted experiments on robot traversable path model predictions 
for various field conditions and navigation line extraction. All experiments were done on the same platform used for 
training (see Sect. 3.5). In this section, we present the accuracy results from semantic segmentation and navigation 
line extraction, including results from the training process. We also compare the different models and navigation 
line extraction techniques, covering both the baseline method and our proposed method. It is crucial to highlight 
that, as previously mentioned, this study utilized three training methods (transfer learning, fine-tuning, and training 
from scratch). However, the results reported here are based on the fine-tuning method since it demonstrated the 
best performance.

4.3  Navigation line extraction
The next step after the segmentation was the navigation line extraction using the obtained mask from the semantic 
segmentation. For a better evaluation, this study implemented the baseline algorithm as described in Sect. 3.7 for com-
parison with our improved algorithm. The performance of both methods was evaluated on the obtained predictions 
from the semantic segmentation experiments. All comparisons were done as described in Sect. 3.7.2. Figure 13 shows 
the ground truth and extracted navigation lines (for both methods) for robot navigation within crop rows under different 
lighting conditions. Although the baseline method demonstrated the best performance under the bright lighting condi-
tion for the ENet model, it was inconsistent across all models and lighting conditions, because of its inability to accurately 
capture the curvature and orientation of the navigation path. In contrast, our proposed improvement consistently and 
accurately predicted the navigation lines across the three models for the different lighting conditions. The predicted 
lines closely matched the ground truth lines, demonstrating the robustness of the improved algorithm.

5  Conclusion and future work
In conclusion, this study has successfully developed and evaluated a robust deep learning-based semantic segmen-
tation approach with a novel navigation line extraction algorithm for autonomous agricultural robots. The research 
addressed the critical challenge of accurate crop row navigation in diverse field conditions, including varying growth 
stages and lighting conditions. By leveraging state-of-the-art semantic segmentation models (ENet, Deeplabv3+, and 
PSPNet) and introducing a novel navigation line extraction method, this study has made significant contributions in 
enhancing the precision and reliability of autonomous navigation in agricultural settings.
The methodology employed a comprehensive approach, encompassing careful dataset preparation, innovative 
data annotation techniques, and strategic model training strategies. The semantic segmentation models demon-
strated impressive performance, with PSPNet achieving the highest mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 96.50%, 
closely followed by Deeplabv3+ at 96.30% and ENet at 95.13%. However, ENet demonstrated a more stable learning 
process, making its predictions more consistent with the ground truth under various lighting conditions. These results 
underscore the models’robustness across various lighting conditions, with all three models performing best under 
normal lighting. The novel navigation line extraction algorithm, an improvement over the baseline Douglas–Peucker 
method, showed remarkable accuracy. It significantly reduced angle errors, with average errors of 1.1°, 1.6°, and 
1.6° for ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet, respectively, compared to 4.6°, 4.9°, and 6.7° with the baseline method. This 
substantial improvement in accuracy is crucial for precise robot navigation within crop rows of corn fields.
While this research has made significant advancements and achieved remarkable performance on the test sce-
narios as presented, there are exciting avenues for future work. Given the limited testing of the proposed algorithm 
on only corn crop and the lighting conditions presented, it is also important to adapt this algorithm to other crop 
environments and conditions such as undulating and bumpy terrains, rocky terrains, irregular road structures, occlu-
sions, obstacles, and other conditions typical of an agricultural field. Hence, future work should consider an extensive 
testing of the proposed algorithm on diverse conditions seen in agricultural fields. This would further validate the 
generalizability of the proposed approach, potentially leading to a universal navigation solution for agricultural 
robots across diverse farming scenarios. For real-time deployment on embedded systems, it is pertinent to evalu-
ate the processing (inference) speed of the developed models in this study. Therefore, future work in this direction 
should consider optimizing the algorithms using accelerator libraries such as TensorRT for efficient deployment on 
embedded systems and to improve the processing speed of the algorithms for real-time processing. Finally, given 
the limitation of the Douglas–Peucker algorithm as it uses a user-defined threshold parameter (epsilon) to determine 
the level of simplification applied to the polygon (navigation path), future studies could explore the application of 
reinforcement learning (RL) techniques to dynamically learn an optimal threshold based on real-time field conditions, 
rather than relying on a fixed, user-defined value. Instead of setting a static epsilon, an RL agent can learn the best 
value based on different environmental conditions. This way, the agent can dynamically adjust epsilon to maintain 
an optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency.

Abstract: In the rapidly evolving field of agriculture, the integration of autonomous systems is essential for enhancing productiv- ity and efficiency. This study addresses the challenge of navigation line extraction in autonomous agricultural robots, a critical component for precise field operations. In this study, three deep learning-based semantic segmentation models, ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet, were trained on corn crop row images to extract the traversable path of the robot. Then, we proposed a novel navigation line extraction algorithm based on the Douglas–Peucker algorithm which uses the output mask from the semantic segmentation to extract the centre navigation line for robot guidance. The results of the experiments showed that PSPNet achieved the highest mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 96.50%, followed by Deeplabv3+ (96.30%) and ENet (95.13%). While ENet showed more consistent performance across various lighting condi- tions, the novel algorithm demonstrated remarkable accuracy, reducing angle errors to an average of 1.1°, 1.6°, and 1.6° for ENet, Deeplabv3+, and PSPNet, respectively, compared to 4.6°, 4.9°, and 6.7° using the baseline method. This improve- ment is critical for ensuring precise and stable robot navigation in agricultural fields. Beyond its technical contributions, this study offers practical implications for real-world deployment, ensuring reliable operation in dynamic agricultural environments. By addressing limitations in conventional navigation techniques, the proposed method enhances robot maneuverability in corn crop fields, particularly under challenging lighting conditions. However, its application across different crop types and terrains, further optimizing real-time processing efficiency, are yet to be explored. This work represents a significant step toward achieving robust, autonomous navigation in precision agriculture.
